lines.text: repeat forever:
pick a state $S$ and an action $A$ at random
ask the sample model for a next reward $R$ and state $S'$
$Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma\max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)]$

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 8.1; check ch08.q-planning confirms it finds an optimal maze policy.

explainer.problem: Plan with a model by learning from simulated experience: the same Q-learning backup, fed by a model instead of the world.

example.text: On the 47-state maze, with the maze itself as the model, 100 random backups leave the greedy policy incomplete; 20,000 give a policy that follows a shortest path (14 steps).

advantages: Any sample model will do; no probabilities needed.
limitations: Uniformly random choice of pairs wastes most backups (§8.4).

comparisons.point: The same backup, applied to real rather than simulated transitions.
Dyna-Q runs this as its planning step, between real steps.

lines.text: Start with $Q(s, a)$ and an empty $Model(s, a)$
repeat forever:
$S \leftarrow$ the current (nonterminal) state; $A \leftarrow$ ε-greedy$(S, Q)$
take $A$; see $R$ and $S'$
direct RL: $Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma\max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)]$
model learning: $Model(S, A) \leftarrow R, S'$ (a deterministic environment)
planning, $n$ times:
$S \leftarrow$ a random previously seen state; $A \leftarrow$ a random action already taken in it
$R, S' \leftarrow Model(S, A)$
$Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma\max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)]$

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 8.4; Example 8.1 is reproduced by checks ch08.dyna-maze and ch08.fig8-6.

explainer.problem: Combine acting, learning a model, learning directly and planning in one on-line agent, so that limited real experience is used many times over.

example.text: Example 8.1 (30 runs): with n = 0, 5 and 50 planning steps the average episode settles near the shortest path (14 steps) after about 29, 6 and 3 episodes (the draft: about 25, 5, 3). Halfway through the second episode, the n = 50 agent already has a greedy action in 18 states; the n = 0 agent in one.

advantages: Far fewer real steps than Q-learning (Figure 8.5).
Always reactive and always planning: planning steps can be interrupted at any time.
limitations: The model is deterministic and table-based.
A model that is wrong in a pessimistic way may never be corrected (§8.3).

comparisons.point: Dyna-Q with n = 0 is one-step Q-learning.
Prioritized sweeping chooses planning backups by urgency instead of at random.

name: Prioritized sweeping (deterministic environment)
inputs: step size $\alpha$, threshold $\theta$, backups per step $n$

lines.text: Start with $Q(s, a)$, $Model(s, a)$ and an empty priority queue
repeat forever:
$S \leftarrow$ the current state; $A \leftarrow policy(S, Q)$; take $A$; see $R$ and $S'$
$Model(S, A) \leftarrow R, S'$
$P \leftarrow |R + \gamma\max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)|$; if $P > \theta$, queue $(S, A)$ with priority $P$
up to $n$ times, while the queue is not empty:
take the top pair $(S, A)$; $R, S' \leftarrow Model(S, A)$
$Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma\max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)]$
for each pair $(\bar S, \bar A)$ predicted to lead to $S$, with predicted reward $\bar R$:
$P \leftarrow |\bar R + \gamma\max_a Q(S, a) - Q(\bar S, \bar A)|$; if $P > \theta$, queue it with priority $P$ (keeping the higher priority if already queued)

verification.note: Compared with the text layer of Figure 8.9; Example 8.4 is reproduced by check ch08.prioritized.

explainer.problem: Spend planning computation where it changes something: on the predecessors of states whose values have just changed, most urgent first.

example.text: On the Dyna maze and its 3 × 3-refined version (423 states), with at most 5 backups per real step, prioritized sweeping needs over 20 times fewer backups than Dyna-Q before its greedy policy is optimal.

advantages: Propagates changes backward efficiently; a decisive advantage on mazes (Example 8.4).
Extends to stochastic environments with full backups from counted transitions.
limitations: Relies on discrete states and explicit predecessors; extending it to function approximation is open (p. 209).

comparisons.point: Dyna-Q picks planning pairs uniformly at random.
Value iteration sweeps all states; prioritized sweeping orders backups by expected change.
